B1C1: All men desire to know by nature; Aristotle traces a hierarchy from sensation to memory, experience, art, and science, arguing that Wisdom is knowledge of first causes and principles, which is why artists who know 'why' are wiser than mere experienced men.
B1C2: Aristotle characterizes the wise man as knowing universal, difficult, exact, and self-sufficient truths, and argues this science of first causes and ends is the most divine and honorable, pursued for its own sake, arising from wonder and ending wonder through understanding causes.
B1C3: Introducing the four causes (essence, matter, moving cause, and final cause/good), Aristotle surveys the earliest material monists like Thales, Anaximenes, Heraclitus, and Empedocles, then Anaxagoras, who introduced reason (nous) as a cause of order beyond mere matter.
B1C4: Aristotle examines Hesiod, Parmenides, and especially Empedocles, who posited love and strife as causes of good and bad, and the atomists Leucippus and Democritus, who explained things through shape, order, and position of indivisible bodies, but none clarified the moving cause well.
B1C5: Aristotle discusses the Pythagoreans, who made number and its elements (odd/even, limit/unlimited) the principles of all things arranged in ten contrary pairs, and the Eleatics Parmenides, Melissus, and Xenophanes, who held reality to be one and unchangeable.
B1C6: Aristotle presents Plato's philosophy as following the Pythagoreans and Heracliteans, positing Forms as causes of sensible things' essence, mathematical objects as intermediates, and the One and the great-and-small (indefinite dyad) as principles of the Forms themselves.
B1C7: Aristotle reviews all prior thinkers and concludes they grasped only the four causes he had already distinguished (matter, moving cause, essence, and good/end), each only partially and vaguely, none stating the essence or final cause with clarity.
B1C8: Aristotle critiques the monists who chose a single corporeal element (fire, water, air, earth) and pluralists like Empedocles and Anaxagoras, and faults the Pythagoreans for treating mathematical principles as though they explained weight, movement, and generation in the physical world.
B1C9: Aristotle's extended critique of the theory of Forms: it multiplies causes without explaining sensible things, faces the 'third man' problem, cannot account for movement or generation, and the reduction of Forms to numbers and geometrical entities (lines from great-and-small) creates further absurdities.
B1C10: Aristotle concludes Book 1 by summarizing that all philosophers sought the same four causes named in the Physics but expressed them vaguely and immaturely, citing Empedocles' unclear grasp of essence via ratio, and announces a review of remaining difficulties (transition to Book 2/3).
B2C1: Aristotle opens Book 2 (Little Alpha) noting truth is both easy and hard to attain collectively; philosophy is knowledge of truth, and since derivative truths depend on their causes, the principles of eternal things must be the most true of all things.
B2C2: Aristotle argues causes cannot regress to infinity in any of the four kinds (material, efficient, final, formal), since an infinite series without a first term would eliminate causation, the good, definition, and the possibility of knowledge itself.
B2C3: Aristotle notes that expectations of argumentative style depend on habituation, and that mathematical precision is appropriate only to immaterial things, not to natural science generally, since nature involves matter; one must first ask what nature is.
B3C1: Opening Book 3 (Beta), Aristotle catalogues roughly fourteen fundamental aporiai (puzzles) to be resolved before proceeding, including how many sciences study the causes, whether substance and axioms are studied by one science, and whether Forms, numbers, and universals are substances.
B3C2: Aristotle works through the first puzzles: whether one science treats all four causes given they aren't contrary, whether unchangeable mathematical objects have final causes, and whether sensible substances alone exist or whether separately existing Forms and mathematical intermediates must also be posited.
B3C3: Aristotle examines whether genera or the parts composing a thing are the true principles and elements, arguing against genera as principles (unity and being cannot be genera since differentiae would then lack them) while noting species predicated of individuals seem closer to principles.
B3C4: Aristotle presses the hardest aporia: if only individuals exist, infinite individuals seem unknowable, but if genera exist apart, that was shown impossible; he also asks whether principles of perishable and imperishable things are the same, criticizing Hesiod's theologians and Empedocles' inconsistency about strife.
B3C5: Aristotle raises the puzzle of whether numbers, bodies, planes, and points are substances, noting that although lines and points seem more fundamental than bodies as their limits, they cannot exist apart from bodies nor undergo genuine generation or destruction, like the 'now' in time.
B3C6: Aristotle closes Book 3 questioning whether Forms are needed beyond perceptible and mathematical objects to secure substances numerically one, whether elements exist potentially or actually, and whether principles are universal (then not a 'this', not substance) or individual (then unknowable without further universals).
B4C1: Aristotle introduces the science of 'being as being,' distinct from the special sciences that each cut off a part of being. This universal science seeks the first principles and highest causes of being qua being itself.
B4C2: Being is said in many senses but all relate to one central point, substance, as the primary sense (like 'healthy' relates to health). Thus one science, first philosophy, studies being, unity, sameness, difference, and contraries as they relate to substance.
B4C3: The philosopher who studies being as being must also investigate the axioms used in all sciences, especially the most certain principle: the same attribute cannot both belong and not belong to the same subject at the same time and in the same respect.
B4C4: Aristotle defends the principle of non-contradiction against those who deny it, arguing it cannot be demonstrated directly but can be shown negatively: any meaningful speech presupposes it, since a word denying all fixed meaning makes reasoning and predication impossible.
B4C5: Aristotle examines Protagoras's doctrine that all appearances are true, tracing it to observations of sensible change and disagreement among perceivers. He argues perception's relativity to observer, organ, and condition does not make all judgments equally true, since some things are unchangeable.
B4C6: Aristotle answers relativists who make everything relative to the perceiver, showing that if things come to be independently of thought, not everything is relative to opinion, and that contraries, like contradictories, cannot simultaneously belong to the same subject.
B4C7: Aristotle argues there is no intermediate between contradictory statements: of any subject one must either affirm or deny a given predicate, since to say something is neither true nor false leads to absurdities and infinite regress.
B4C8: Concluding the book, Aristotle refutes the extreme views that nothing is true or that everything is true, and that all things are at rest or all in motion, showing each is self-refuting and inconsistent with the existence of an unmoved first mover.
B5C1: Lexicon entry on 'beginning' (arche): distinguishes senses including a thing's starting point, the best point to start learning from, an immanent originating part, an external originating cause, that which directs change by will, and the ground from which a thing is known.
B5C2: Lexicon entry on 'cause': distinguishes the four causes—material, formal, efficient, and final—and notes causes can be proper or accidental, prior or posterior, potential or actual, and that the same thing can cause contraries by its presence or absence.
B5C3: Lexicon entry on 'element': the primary, indivisible-in-kind component immanent in a thing, as letters are elements of speech; by extension, anything small, simple, and widely applicable, such as unity, the point, or genera, is also called an element.
B5C4: Lexicon entry on 'nature' (physis): senses include the genesis of growing things, the immanent source of growth, the primary matter of natural things, and especially the essence or form of natural objects that is the source of their own movement.
B5C5: Lexicon entry on 'necessary': distinguishes what is required for life or good, the compulsory that opposes purpose, and, most strictly, that which cannot be otherwise; eternal unmovable things are necessary without compulsion since they admit no other state.
B5C6: Lexicon entry on 'one': catalogs senses of unity—accidental unity, unity by continuity, by having an indivisible substratum in kind, by common genus, and by indivisible definition—and correspondingly distinguishes numerical, specific, generic, and analogical oneness.
B5C7: Lexicon entry on 'being': distinguishes accidental being (predicates coinciding in one subject), essential being corresponding to the categories, being as signifying truth of a statement, and being as potential versus actual.
B5C8: Lexicon entry on 'substance': senses include simple bodies not predicated of a subject, the cause of a thing's being (like soul), the defining limiting parts of a thing, and the essence expressed in a definition; ultimately substance means either ultimate substratum or separable form.
B5C9: Lexicon entry on 'the same,' 'other,' 'different,' and 'like': the same is distinguished as accidental sameness versus essential sameness (identity of matter or essence); other and different are explained as its opposites, and like as sharing the same or predominant qualities.
B5C10: Lexicon entry on 'opposite': covers contradictories, contraries, relatives, and privation/possession. Contrary is defined through several related senses as the greatest difference within a genus, kind, faculty, or recipient subject, correlating with 'same' and 'other' in species.
B5C11: Lexicon entry on 'prior' and 'posterior': distinguishes priority in place, time, movement, power, and arrangement, priority in knowledge (universal versus perceptual), priority of attributes, and priority in nature/substance (what can exist independently of what).
B5C12: Lexicon entry on 'potency' (dynamis): defines it as a source of change in another thing or in itself qua other, covering active and passive capacities, capacity to act well, and states of resisting change; correspondingly defines the possible and impossible/necessary.
B5C13: Lexicon entry on 'quantum': that which is divisible into parts each a 'one' and 'this'; distinguishes plurality (numerable, discontinuous) from magnitude (measurable, continuous—length, breadth, depth), and things quantitative essentially versus incidentally.
B5C14: Lexicon entry on 'quality': senses include the differentia of a thing's essence (e.g., two-footed for man), a mathematical sense applying to numbers, the changeable modifications of moving substances (like heat and color), and quality as virtue or vice.
B5C15: Lexicon entry on 'relative': three kinds—numerical relations (double to half), active-to-passive relations (heating to being heated), and measure-to-measurable relations (knowledge to the knowable)—the last differing because the correlative does not itself refer back.
B5C16: Lexicon entry on 'complete' (teleion): that outside which no part can be found, that which cannot be excelled in goodness within its kind, and that which has attained its proper end; the sense is extended ironically to describe complete badness as well.
B5C17: Lexicon entry on 'limit': the outermost point of a thing beyond which no part exists, the form of a magnitude, the end (telos) toward which movement or action tends, and the essence or definition, which is the limit of knowledge of a thing.
B5C18: Lexicon entry on 'that in virtue of which' (kath' ho) and 'in virtue of itself' (kath' hauto): the former parallels the senses of cause (form, subject, purpose, ground of inference); the latter covers essence, genus-membership, direct attributes, self-caused features, and unique properties.
B5C19: Lexicon entry on 'disposition' (diathesis): the arrangement of a thing's parts in respect of place, potency, or kind, implying some definite positional ordering of the parts of that which has parts.
B5C20: Lexicon entry on 'having'/'habit' (hexis): an activity-like relation between haver and thing had (as with wearing a garment), a disposition by which something is well or ill disposed in itself or relatively (like health), and a partial instance of such disposition.
B5C21: Lexicon entry on 'affection' (pathos): a quality by which a thing can be altered (such as color or taste), the actualized alteration itself, especially harmful alterations and injuries, and, in an extended sense, serious misfortunes.
B5C22: Lexicon entry on 'privation': distinguishes lacking an attribute a class naturally has though the individual would not (a plant lacking eyes), lacking what one's own nature would have, lacking it at the natural time to have it, and forcible removal of an attribute.
B5C23: Lexicon entry on 'to have'/'to hold': senses include treating something according to one's own impulse (fever having a man), being the receptive subject of a form or affection, containing as a vessel contains liquid, and preventing something from moving according to its own impulse.
B5C24: Lexicon entry on 'to come from something': covers coming from matter (genus or proximate), from a moving/originating principle, from a compound as part from whole, from form as part of the composite, and in a looser sense mere temporal succession.
B5C25: Lexicon entry on 'part': senses include any division of a quantum, only the measuring divisions of a quantum, the elements composing a formed whole (matter and form), and the constituent notions within a thing's defining formula, such as genus being part of species.
B5C26: Lexicon entry on 'a whole': that from which none of its natural parts is missing, and that which unifies its contained parts into one, either severally or jointly; distinguishes 'whole' (where position matters) from mere 'total' (where it does not), like water or number.
B5C27: Discusses 'mutilated' as applying only to a divisible whole whose essence persists after loss, and only when a defining, non-regenerating extremity with fixed position is removed—so numbers, water, and baldness do not count as mutilation.
B5C28: Lexicon entry on 'race' or 'genus': senses include continuous generation of things sharing form, descent from a common originator (like Hellenes from Hellen), the underlying kind for figures (plane, solid), and the genus term in a definition, as opposed to differing in genus.
B5C29: Lexicon entry on 'the false': applies to things that cannot be combined as stated or that produce a deceptive appearance (like a dream), to false accounts describing something other than what they truly fit, and to a 'false man' who delights in deceptive speech.
B5C30: Lexicon entry on 'accident': that which attaches to a subject neither of necessity nor usually and has no definite cause, such as finding treasure while digging; and, in a second sense, what attaches to a thing in virtue of itself but is not part of its essence, like a triangle's angles summing to two right angles.
B6C1: Aristotle distinguishes theoretical sciences by their objects: physics studies movable, matter-involved substance; mathematics studies the immovable but not separately existing; a first science (theology) must study what is both eternal, immovable, and separable, making it universal by being first and the study of being qua being.
B6C2: Aristotle argues the accidental (that which is neither always nor for the most part) cannot be an object of science, since all science concerns what is invariable or usual; the accidental arises from matter capable of being otherwise and has no determinate cause.
B6C3: Aristotle examines whether all future events are necessitated by chains of prior causes, concluding that some events trace back to a starting-point that is itself fortuitous, the origin of chance, rather than being wholly necessitated.
B6C4: Aristotle sets aside 'being' as accidental and 'being' as truth, since the latter is a matter of combination and separation in thought, not in things themselves, leaving being qua being as the proper subject for the inquiry into substance that follows.
B7C1: Aristotle opens Book Seven by declaring substance the primary sense of being, prior to all other categories in definition, knowledge, and time; the ancient question 'what is being?' is really the question 'what is substance?', making substance the central object of inquiry.
B7C2: Aristotle surveys prior views on substance, noting sensible bodies (animals, elements, heavenly bodies) are commonly deemed substances, while Plato and Speusippus posited additional substances (Forms, mathematical objects, numbers), setting up the need to examine sensible substance first.
B7C3: Substance is said in four ways: essence, universal, genus, and substratum. Examining the substratum, Aristotle finds matter stripped of all qualities seems to be substance, yet rejects this since separability and thisness belong properly to form, turning inquiry toward sensible substances.
B7C4: Aristotle defines essence as what a thing is 'propter se' (in virtue of itself), distinguishing it from accidental compounds like 'white man'; strictly speaking only species have a true essence and definition, though quality and quantity have essence in a secondary, derivative sense.
B7C5: Examining compounds like 'snub' (concavity-in-a-nose), Aristotle shows such terms cannot be defined without repetition or infinite regress, concluding that in the strict sense only substance is definable, while other categories require definition by addition of a determinant.
B7C6: Aristotle argues that for primary, self-subsistent things a thing and its essence are one and the same, since to know a thing is to know its essence; separating them, as with Platonic Forms, leads to infinite regress and severs knowledge from its objects.
B7C7: Aristotle analyzes production: things come to be by nature, art, or spontaneity, always involving matter (that from which) and form (that toward which); art's form pre-exists in the maker's soul, and generation proceeds by thought reducing means to an achievable starting point.
B7C8: Aristotle argues that form itself is never generated, only the composite of form and matter (e.g. a brazen sphere) comes to be; the maker brings form into pre-existing matter, so Platonic Forms are unnecessary since the begetter, being of the same form, suffices to produce the product.
B7C9: Aristotle explains why some things arise both by art and spontaneously (like health) while others (like a house) do not, based on whether their matter can move itself in the required way; in all cases substance/form is the starting point from which production proceeds.
B7C10: Aristotle asks whether the formula of a whole must include formulae of its parts, distinguishing material parts (posterior, part of the concrete compound, like flesh and bones) from formal parts (which may be prior, part of the definition, like the soul relative to the animal).
B7C11: Aristotle addresses which parts belong to form versus to the concrete material compound, criticizing those who reduce geometric figures or man to numbers or eliminate matter entirely; sensible things like animals cannot be defined without reference to matter and movement.
B7C12: Aristotle investigates the unity of definitions (e.g. 'two-footed animal'), arguing through the method of division that a proper definition, obtained by dividing differentia by differentia, ends in a single last differentia that constitutes the form and substance of the thing.
B7C13: Aristotle argues at length that no universal (like 'animal') can be a substance, since substance is proper to one thing while universals are common to many, are predicated of a subject, and cannot themselves be composed of other substances in complete actuality.
B7C14: Aristotle presses the argument against Platonists who make Forms substances composed of genus and differentiae, showing that if 'animal' is one thing shared by man and horse, or many, either way absurdities follow, refuting separately existing Forms of sensible things.
B7C15: Aristotle contends that sensible individual substances, having matter capable of being and not being, admit no definition or demonstration, only formulae of their universal being; likewise Platonic Ideas, if individuals, cannot be defined since definitions necessarily use common, shareable terms.
B7C16: Aristotle notes that even things thought to be substances, like the parts of animals and the elements earth, fire, air, are mere potentialities apart from actualizing unity; he reaffirms that neither unity, being, nor universals are substances, and no substance is composed of substances.
B7C17: Taking a fresh approach, Aristotle argues substance is the cause of a compound's being one thing rather than a mere heap (e.g. why bricks and stones are a house); this cause is form or essence, itself a principle rather than an element, since analyzing composites into elements alone leaves that unifying 'something else' unexplained.
B8C1: Aristotle reviews prior conclusions on substance: sensible substances all have matter, and substance is analyzed as matter (potential 'this'), form or shape, or the compound of both, which alone is generated and destroyed.
B8C2: Turning to actuality in sensible things, Aristotle rejects Democritus's three differentiae (shape, position, order) as too narrow, showing things differ by composition, position, time, place, and quality; being means different things for each definition of matter plus actuality.
B8C3: Aristotle asks whether names signify the composite, the form, or both, arguing essence attaches to form/actuality; a syllable or house is not merely its elements plus juxtaposition but something further, the substance, comparing substance's unity to number's.
B8C4: Discussing material causes, Aristotle notes each thing has matter proper to it and one thing can arise from another in different senses; for eternal natural substances (like eclipses) causes must be sought without matter, using proximate formal and moving causes.
B8C5: Aristotle explains that only things which come to be and change have matter; he examines how matter relates to contrary states (health/disease, wine/vinegar), showing potentiality for a contrary is not identical with being the matter of it.
B8C6: Returning to the problem of definitional unity, Aristotle argues the cause of a thing's oneness (e.g., 'animal' plus 'biped' making one man) is that matter is potentially and form is actually the same thing, dissolving the need for 'participation' or 'communion' theories.
B9C1: Opening Book 9, Aristotle turns from substance to potency (dunamis) and actuality, distinguishing the strict, motion-related sense of potency as an originative source of change in another thing or in itself as other, plus potency for acting/being acted on well or badly.
B9C2: Aristotle distinguishes rational potencies (arts/sciences), which can produce contrary effects because guided by a formula, from non-rational potencies, which produce only one effect each; science requires desire or choice to determine which contrary outcome occurs.
B9C3: Aristotle refutes the Megarians, who claim a thing 'can' act only while actually acting; he shows this destroys change, becoming, and the arts, proving potency and actuality must be distinct and a capable thing need not always be exercising its capacity.
B9C4: Aristotle clarifies that 'capable of being' does not mean 'will be'; he distinguishes the impossible from the merely false, and formally establishes that if A's reality entails B's reality, then A's possibility entails B's possibility.
B9C5: Aristotle explains potencies arise by nature, practice, or learning; rational potencies (which can produce contrary effects) require desire or will to decide which effect occurs when agent and patient meet under the right conditions, while non-rational ones act automatically.
B9C6: Aristotle defines actuality by analogy (building is to able-to-build as waking is to sleeping) rather than by strict definition, and distinguishes incomplete movements (which aim at an end not yet reached) from complete actualities (like seeing or living) present all at once.
B9C7: Aristotle specifies precisely when a thing exists potentially rather than merely by analogy of names: something is potentially X only once its proximate matter is disposed such that nothing external need be added, removed, or changed for it to become X.
B9C8: Aristotle argues actuality is prior to potency in formula (potency is defined through actuality), in time (an actual thing always precedes a potential one of the same kind), and in substantiality, since actuality is the end for whose sake potency exists.
B9C9: Aristotle contends actuality is better and more valuable than potency, since potency is indifferently capable of good or bad while actuality is determinately one; hence eternal, imperishable things, having no potentiality for non-being, are actual and free of defect.
B9C10: Aristotle treats being and non-being as truth and falsity: for composite things truth is combining/separating judgment correctly, but for simple, incomposite essences there is no falsity, only contact (knowing) or non-contact (ignorance), since such things cannot be otherwise.
B10C1: Opening Book 10 on unity, Aristotle enumerates senses of 'one' (continuous, whole, individual, indivisible in kind) and argues that to be one is essentially to be a measure, most properly of quantity, the indivisible starting point by which a kind is known.
B10C2: Aristotle argues unity, like being, cannot itself be a separate substance or genus; in each category the 'one' is some definite thing (e.g., white among colors), so 'to be one' just means to be one particular thing, not unity as such.
B10C3: Aristotle analyzes the one and the many as contraries corresponding to indivisible and divisible, then distinguishes senses of 'same', 'like', and 'other', showing genuine difference (as opposed to mere otherness) requires an underlying genus shared by the differing things.
B10C4: Aristotle argues contrariety is complete difference, the greatest difference between things in the same genus or species, and shows every contrariety ultimately reduces to and is grounded in the primary opposition of positive state and privation.
B10C5: Aristotle asks how 'equal' opposes 'great' and 'small', concluding it is not contrary to either alone but is a privative negation of both together, functioning as an intermediate between them rather than as a standard contrary.
B10C6: Aristotle examines how the one opposes the many, distinguishing 'many' as excessive plurality (opposed to 'few') from 'many' as number (opposed to 'one' as measure to thing measured), correcting Anaxagoras's confused talk of boundlessness in smallness.
B10C7: Aristotle argues that intermediates between contraries must belong to the same genus as those contraries and must themselves be composed out of the contraries, since change passes through them and they possess degrees of each extreme.
B10C8: Aristotle defines being 'other in species' as having contrariety within a shared genus at the level of definition, distinguishing genuine specific difference (like horse versus man) from mere numerical or material difference among individuals of the same species.
B10C9: Aristotle explains why male and female, though contrary, do not make man and woman different species: their difference lies in the matter (the body) rather than in the definitional essence, unlike genuine specific differences such as footed versus winged.
B10C10: Aristotle concludes that since perishable and imperishable are contraries belonging necessarily (not accidentally) to the things that have them, perishable and imperishable things must differ in kind, refuting Platonic Forms that would make individuals of one Form both perishable and imperishable.
B11C1: Raises aporiai about Wisdom: is it one science or many, does it treat all substances or attributes too, and whether it deals with perceptible things, Forms, or mathematical objects, none of which seem satisfactory subjects.
B11C2: Continues the puzzles: whether a separable substance exists apart from sensibles, whether one or many such principles exist, whether being and unity can be substances or genera, and how a science of universals can know the particular first principle.
B11C3: Argues being is said in many senses but all refer to one common thing (like 'medical'), so a single science, philosophy, can study being qua being and its contraries, resolving the aporia of one science covering many genera.
B11C4: Explains that first philosophy examines the common axioms mathematics merely applies in restricted domains; physics and mathematics are thus parts of Wisdom, studying being qua moving or qua quantity rather than qua being.
B11C5: Defends the principle of non-contradiction: the same thing cannot both be and not be at once; argues by refutation that any speaker who denies this destroys meaningful discourse itself.
B11C6: Refutes Protagoras's 'man is the measure' relativism and Heraclitean flux doctrines, arguing sensation and change presuppose enduring, determinate natures, so contradictory statements cannot both be true of the same subject.
B11C7: Distinguishes three theoretical sciences - physics, mathematics, and theology - ranking theology highest since it studies separable, unmovable, divine substance; asks whether the science of being qua being is universal or restricted to this highest class.
B11C8: Argues there can be no science of the accidental, since accidents occur neither always nor for the most part nor of necessity; also distinguishes accidental being and being as truth from essential being, which alone has causes worth seeking.
B11C9: Defines movement as the actuality of what exists potentially, qua potential (e.g., building is the actuality of the buildable), showing why movement is hard to classify yet real, and locates movement in the movable thing itself.
B11C10: Argues the infinite cannot exist actually or as a separate substance, whether as body or number, since an infinite body could have no coherent place, rest, or motion; infinity belongs only accidentally to some underlying thing.
B11C11: Classifies change as accidental or essential, and essential change as occurring only between positive contrary terms, excluding generation/destruction (change to/from non-being) from true 'movement' properly speaking.
B11C12: Argues movement occurs only in quality, quantity, and place, not in substance, relation, or action/passion, since there can be no 'movement of movement'; also defines togetherness, contact, succession, and continuity in terms of place.
B12C1: Opens the study of substance, ranking it prior to all other categories, and distinguishes three kinds of substance: perishable sensible, eternal sensible, and immovable substance, the last belonging to a science beyond physics.
B12C2: Shows sensible substance is changeable and requires an underlying matter that persists through change between contraries, concluding that generation proceeds from what exists potentially rather than from sheer non-being.
B12C3: Argues that matter and form themselves do not come to be, only composites do; distinguishes matter, form (the 'this' toward which change moves), and the composite particular, and denies Forms are needed since man begets man.
B12C4: Asks whether all things share the same causes and elements; concludes causes are the same only analogically (form, privation, matter) across categories, with each class having its own specific form, privation, and matter.
B12C5: Extends the analogy of actuality and potentiality as causes across different things, stressing that proximate causes are always particular individuals (Peleus causes Achilles), while universal causes exist only analogically.
B12C6: Argues there must be an eternal unmovable substance whose essence is pure actuality, since movement and time are eternal and potency alone cannot explain why movement always occurs; criticizes theories deriving being from potency or chaos.
B12C7: Presents the unmoved mover as an eternal, immaterial, unchangeable substance that moves the heavens as an object of love and desire; identifies this mover with God, whose life is eternal self-contemplative thought, the best and most pleasant activity.
B12C8: Considers how many unmovable substances/movers are needed to account for the distinct eternal motions of the stars and planets, surveying Eudoxus's and Callippus's astronomical spheres, and affirms the ancient tradition that these first substances are divine.
B12C9: Examines the nature of divine thought, concluding that since it must think the most excellent object, God's thinking must be self-directed - 'thinking on thinking' - so that thought and its object are identical and undivided.
B12C10: Asks how the universe contains the good, as both separate leader and immanent order, comparing it to an army or household; criticizes earlier philosophers' accounts of contraries, becoming, and plural principles, ending with 'the rule of many is not good; one ruler let there be.'
B13C1: Aristotle introduces the inquiry into whether immovable, eternal substances exist beyond sensibles, framing two rival views to examine: that mathematical objects are substances, and that the Ideas are substances.
B13C2: Aristotle argues mathematical objects cannot exist within sensible things (leading to absurd infinite regresses of planes, lines, points) nor separately from them, since separation makes them wrongly prior in being to magnitudes.
B13C3: Aristotle resolves the puzzle: mathematical objects exist not separately but as sensible things considered qua quantity, through abstraction; mathematics is precise because it studies things apart from movement, and it also treats the beautiful via order and symmetry.
B13C4: Aristotle traces the origin of the Ideal theory to Socrates' universal definitions combined with Heraclitean flux, then argues none of the arguments proving Forms exist are convincing, and shows the theory generates unwanted Forms of relations and negations.
B13C5: Aristotle asks what Forms actually contribute to sensible things, arguing they cause neither motion nor being nor knowledge, that calling them 'patterns' is empty metaphor, and that things can come to be without any Form to copy.
B13C6: Aristotle surveys the possible ways numbers could be constituted (associable or inassociable units, ideal vs mathematical number) among those who make number a separable substance, setting up the difficulties to follow, including the Pythagorean view.
B13C7: Aristotle examines whether units are associable or inassociable, showing both options lead to absurdities: associable units collapse Ideas into mathematical number, while inassociable units make ideal numbers impossible to generate consistently or relate to one another.
B13C8: Aristotle asks what differentiates one unit or number from another, finding neither quantity nor quality works, and shows that whether number is finite or infinite, or capped at ten as some hold, the theory produces paradoxes like an infinite supply of 'man-himself'.
B13C9: Aristotle extends the critique to lines, planes, and solids built from the 'great and small,' showing the same generative difficulties as with number, and concludes number and magnitudes cannot exist apart from things; he reviews how Forms became conflated with universals.
B13C10: Aristotle raises the dilemma that if principles/elements of substances are individual they yield unknowable multiplicities, but if universal they make non-substance prior to substance, resolving it by distinguishing potential (universal) from actual (particular) knowledge.
B14C1: Aristotle argues no contrary can be an ultimate first principle since contraries require an underlying subject, then criticizes those who make the 'unequal' or 'great and small' matter for the One, since relatives cannot be substances or genuine elements.
B14C2: Aristotle contends eternal things cannot be composed of elements since anything composite could in principle not exist, then traces the Platonists' need to admit non-being (following Parmenides) to explain plurality, questioning how being and non-being combine to produce many substances.
B14C3: Aristotle argues the Pythagoreans reasonably treat numbers as constituting things but err in making bodies literally composed of numbers, while those positing separate mathematical number cannot explain its relation to Ideal number or how it is generated.
B14C4: Aristotle addresses whether the good is among the first principles or arises later, arguing it is absurd to make the One (source of goodness) generate its contrary as the bad, since this would make plurality itself the origin of evil.
B14C5: Aristotle objects that first principles of the universe cannot be indefinite/incomplete like animal seed since actual complete things (a man) always precede, and shows no proposed mode of number's generation from elements (intermixture, juxtaposition, contrariety) is coherent.
B14C6: Aristotle dismisses numerological correlations (seven strings, seven Pleiades, musical ratios) as coincidental resemblances rather than causes, concluding that numbers cannot be agents, matter, form, or final cause, and that the whole theory of separable numbers fails.
